messages.subject: Local Linear Trend model issues
parts:
I'm dipping my toes into some time series modelling, but I've run into issues with creating a local linear trend model. 

The model I would like to build is basically:

y_t = u_t + e_obs,  e_obs ~ N(0, s_obs)

u_[t + 1] = u_t + v_t + e_level,  e_level ~ N(0, s_level)

v[t + 1] = v_t ~ e_slope,  e_slope ~ N(0, s_slope)


And this is my (naive) attempt to translate it to stan code

data {
  int T;
  vector[T] y;
}
parameters {
  vector[T] u; // Level
  vector[T] v; // Slope
  real<lower=0> s_obs;
  real<lower=0> s_level;
  real<lower=0> s_slope;
}
model {
  y ~ normal(u, s_obs);
  for(t in 2:T) {
      u[t] ~ normal(u[t - 1] + v[t - 1], s_level);
      v[t] ~ normal(v[t - 1], s_slope);
  }

  u[1] ~ normal(0, s_level*10); //Added a magnitude, since the ts can start "anywhere"
  v[1] ~ normal(0, s_slope);
  s_obs ~ cauchy(0, 1);
  s_level ~ cauchy(0, 1);
  s_slope ~ cauchy(0, 1);
}

When I fit that to the attached ts the chains looks horrible, with divergent transitions, estimated Bayesian Fraction of Missing Information to low, and low neff and high rhats... My intuition says that there are a lot of parameters to estimate and that it I'm not sure how identifiable this model is, but I'm not sure how to fix that?
And in general if anyone have any tips on literature(papers, blogs etc) on state space time series modelling with Stan that would be super!

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Local Linear Trend model issues
parts:
You’ll probably want to non-center the time series.
For example, instead of

v_t ~ normal(v_{t -1}, s_slope)

you’d do

eta_t ~ normal(0, 1)
v_t = s_slope _ v_{t-1}

Doing that for s will force you to change your model,
but you might want to do that anyways as s_level
may be poorly identified whereas the individual
variations on u and v may be better identified.

messages.author: 497eb9c410b69640
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Local Linear Trend model issues
parts: I don't really understand what you mean, but if I were to write this model non-centered I would write something like:

data {
  int T;
  vector[T] y;
}
parameters {

vector[T] u_raw;
  vector[T] v_raw;

real<lower=0> s_obs;
  real<lower=0> s_level;
  real<lower=0> s_slope;
}

vector[T] u; // Level
  vector[T] v; // Slope

u[1] = u_raw[1] * s_level;
  v[1] = v_raw[1] * s_slope;
  for(t in 2:T) {
    u[t] = (u_raw[t] + u[t - 1] + v[t - 1]) * s_level;
    v[t] =  (v_raw[t] + v[t - 1]) * s_slope;

u_raw ~ normal(0, 1); // Should imply u[t] ~ N(u[t-1] + v[t-1], s_level)
  v_raw ~ normal(0, 1); // Should imply v[t] ~ N(v[t-1], s_slope)

s_obs ~ cauchy(0, 1);
  s_level ~ cauchy(0, 1);
  s_slope ~ cauchy(0, 1);
}

When I do that I get rid of divergent transitions, but three out of four chains still ended up with "Bayesian Fraction of Missing Information was low", and neff was around 2 for most parameters. I would be most grateful if you could elaborate a bit more on how to "fix" this model.

Thanks in advance

/Jon

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Local Linear Trend model issues [low BFMI persists on reparameterization?]
parts:
If n_eff = 2, you can't trust any of the other stats.

What happens to the parameter estimates? What do the
traceplots look like? Those priors allow very extreme
values, but it looks like the continuou multiplication by s_level
and s_slope may require its value to be relatively low.

With all that addition, are you sure the model's identified?

Can you fit simulated data?

- Bob
